# Technological Singularity
The concept of the technological singularity—the ultra-rapid advent of superhuman intelligence—has deep historical roots, with discussions dating back to John von Neumann's notion of an essential singularity. I. J. Good formalized the idea in 1965, speculating that an "intelligence explosion" would occur when an ultraintelligent machine could design even better machines, leaving human intelligence far behind. Vernor Vinge later popularized the term "singularity," describing it as a transition similar to the center of a black hole, which would signal the end of the human era as a new superintelligence continuously upgrades itself.
The singularity is intrinsically linked to the concept of recursive self-improvement, where an AI, once capable of matching or surpassing human creators, could autonomously improve its own software and hardware. While some futurists predict specific timelines for its arrival (e.g., Kurzweil predicting by 2045), others dispute its plausibility due to technological limitations or philosophical arguments. The potential impacts are vast, ranging from solving major global problems to posing existential risks, which necessitates ongoing research into aligning AI goal-systems with human values.
